key.title: Songs of Kabir: Poems I–XV
key.main_idea: In these poems Kabir says the Divine is not found in temples, mosques, rituals or caste, but within each person and in this life. He invites the seeker to look inward with love, here and now, rather than waiting for death or outer ceremonies.

key_lessons.text: The Divine is close, "beside thee", and not limited to any place of worship or ritual.
key_lessons.source_snippet: I am neither in temple nor in mosque: I am neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash

key_lessons.text: Caste and religion do not decide who is a true seeker; people of every background have found God.
key_lessons.source_snippet: It is needless to ask of a saint the caste to which he belongs

key_lessons.text: Seek and understand while you are alive; Kabir doubts that what is not found in life will be found after death.
key_lessons.source_snippet: hope for Him whilst you live, know whilst you live, understand whilst you live

key_lessons.text: What we search for outside is already within us, like the musk the deer seeks in the grass.
key_lessons.source_snippet: The musk is in the deer, but it seeks it not within itself: it wanders in quest of grass.

key_lessons.text: Love, not argument or display, is the heart of the path.

key.takeaway: Kabir's invitation is to stop searching only outside, in places and ceremonies, and to look within, with love, today.

quick_check.question: Where does Kabir say the Divine is to be found?
options: Within the seeker, here and now
Only in a particular temple or mosque
quick_check.simpler_explanation: Kabir says God is not limited to temples, mosques or rituals. The Divine is close, within each person, and can be found in this life.

reflection_questions: Where do you usually look for peace or meaning: in places, in people, or within yourself?
Kabir says the musk is in the deer but it searches the grass. What are you searching for outside that might already be within you?
What would it mean for you to "seek while you live", today rather than someday?
key.coverage_note: Translated by Rabindranath Tagore (1915). The lesson explains what the poems say and how they are commonly understood; readers of different traditions may read them differently.

complete.title: Songs of Kabir: Poems I–XV
complete.main_idea: In these poems Kabir says the Divine is not found in temples, mosques, rituals or caste, but within each person and in this life. He invites the seeker to look inward with love, here and now, rather than waiting for death or outer ceremonies.

sections.heading: "Lo! I am beside thee" (Poem I)
sections.explanation: The first poem speaks in the voice of the Divine: you need not search far, for I am right beside you. Not in temple or mosque, not in Kaaba or Kailash, not in rituals, yoga or renunciation. A true seeker meets the Divine in a moment.

examples.source_snippet: O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee.

sections.heading: Beyond caste and creed (Poem II)
sections.explanation: Kabir says it is foolish to ask a saint's caste. People of every occupation and both Hindus and Muslims have reached the same goal, where no mark of difference remains.

examples.text: He names ordinary working people as seekers.
examples.source_snippet: The barber has sought God, the washerwoman, and the carpenter

sections.heading: Seek while you live (Poem III)
sections.explanation: Kabir urges the seeker to hope, know and understand in this life, because "in life deliverance abides". If the bonds are not broken while living, he asks, what hope is there in death? It is the spirit of the quest that helps.

examples.source_snippet: hope for Him whilst you live, know whilst you live, understand whilst you live

sections.heading: The garden within (Poems IV, VI, VIII)
sections.explanation: Several poems turn the search inward: the garden of flowers is in your own body; the moon and sun shine within; within this "earthen vessel" are groves, oceans and stars, and the Creator. The deer seeks musk in the grass, never realising it carries the scent itself.

examples.source_snippet: The musk is in the deer, but it seeks it not within itself: it wanders in quest of grass.

sections.heading: Letting go is gradual (Poem V)
sections.explanation: Kabir is honest about how hard renunciation is: drop one attachment and another appears, from passion to anger to greed to pride. "The true path is rarely found." This is a humane picture of spiritual effort, not a demand for instant perfection.

examples.text: His list of attachments that remain.
examples.source_snippet: So, when I give up passion, I see that anger remains

sections.heading: One reality, and the way of love (Poems VII, IX–XV)
sections.explanation: Kabir describes the creature and the Divine as "ever distinct, yet ever united", like a river and its waves. Words cannot fully describe this. What opens the way is love: "he understands who loves".

examples.source_snippet: The river and its waves are one
